newsitem.title: UK: Central London at standstill after bomb warnings.
newsitem.headline: Central London at standstill after bomb warnings.

text.p: Central London was at a virtual standstill on Monday after suspected IRA bomb warnings closed five main railway stations in the capital as well as Heathrow, Gatwick and Luton airports, police said.
Police said they received telephone calls at the start of the Monday morning rush hour carrying a codeword normally associated with the Irish Republican Army.
The calls warned of devices in stations in the heart of the capital, which carry millions of commuters to work, and its three main airports.

It was not clear whether any devices were found but police were forced to evacuate stations at King's Cross, Charing Cross, Paddington and St Pancras as well as the busy Baker Street underground railway station.
Surrounding roads were closed off while police searched the huge stations, turning the normally bustling heart of the capital into an eerie deserted landscape.
"You can almost hear a pin drop in Trafalgar Square," said one BBC reporter. "Everything is deathly calm".
Traffic on roads and motorways leading into Europe's largest city was at a standstill and the capital was heading for gridlock. Travel organisations advised people not to come into the city.
The bomb threats coincided with Queen Elizabeth's 71st birthday and followed two IRA explosions and a series of hoax calls on Friday which paralysed road and rail links in northern England.
The IRA has stepped up its campaign against British rule of Northern Ireland in the runup to Britain's May 1 national election.

British transport police said coded warnings were received at all five London railway stations around 0715 a.m. (0815 gmt). Police spokesmen in areas covering the airports also said the warnings contained a recognised codeword.
"This is causing massive disruption. It has been timed just as the morning rush hour is about to hit its peak," said Railtrack spokesman Roger Shire.
Hundreds of thousands of commuters were stranded on trains, stuck in traffic jams or being kept behind police barriers unable to reach their places of work.
The bomb warnings formed part of a new campaign by the IRA in mainland Britain to cause huge disruption and maximum publicity at virtually no cost.
Earlier this month the Grand National steeplechase -- one of Britain's biggest sporting events -- was abandoned because of an IRA hoax call to the racecourse minutes before the start.

The attacks appear to be an attempt by the guerrillas to push the issue of Northern Ireland up the British election agenda. Peace talks, from which the IRA's political wing Sinn Fein were excluded, have been suspended during the election campaign.
